body_text:
Let $U \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ be an open set and let $f: U \to \mathbb{C}$. The function
$f$ is *complex differentiable* at a point $z_0 \in U$ if there exists a complex number
$f'(z_0) \in \mathbb{C}$ such that for every $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists $\delta > 0$
such that for all $h \in \mathbb{C}$ with $0 < |h| < \delta$,
$$ \left| \frac{f(z_0 + h) - f(z_0)}{h} - f'(z_0) \right| < \varepsilon. $$
Equivalently, $f$ admits the first-order Taylor expansion:
$$ f(z_0 + h) = f(z_0) + f'(z_0) h + \eta(h) h, \quad \text{where } \lim_{h \to 0} \eta(h) = 0. $$
The function $f$ is said to be *holomorphic* (or *analytic*) on $U$ if it is complex
differentiable at every point of $U$. If $f$ is holomorphic on the entire complex plane
$\mathbb{C}$, it is called *entire*.
